claim: Recall depends on whether the test cue was encoded with the target: a weak cue seen at study (W-W 15.7 vs 10.7 uncued) beats an unstudied strong or weak cue (O-W 11.1 vs 14.1; S-W 9.2 vs 12.2).
agent_test: Store the same note once keyed by writing-time context; retrieve with (a) the writing-time cue and (b) a fresh related cue; compare at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: The strong-cue failure in Thomson and Tulving is partly a report effect: in free report strong cues did not beat no cue (.24-.29 weak vs .08 none), but with forced report both cue types beat no cue (.25-.31 vs .08). Warning subjects that cues are associates lifted 5.33 to 10.07 words (Santa and Lamwers).
agent_test: Compare free-answer vs forced-answer-then-score retrieval from a mismatched cue; score accuracy and calibration separately.
audit_note: All numbers verified in Higham (2002); a14 and b15 are the same paper and Santa and Lamwers (1974) was only checked second-hand through Higham's account, so the claim rests on one paper (single lab).

claim: Environmental (global room) context dependence is small on average: weighted d=.28 (95% CI +-.05, 93 effects, heterogeneous), about .23 for plain reinstatement.
agent_test: Do not spend tokens on global context match; test only per-item cue match.
audit_note: Smith and Vela (2001) numbers verified (d=.28 +-.05, 93 effects, QT=242.47, reinstatement .23); a12 and b01/b02 are the same paper, and the paper stresses effects are not always modest (18 of 93 exceeded d=.80, interference-reduction d=.68). Murre check not opened.

claim: The Godden and Baddeley diver result did not replicate in the one close replication (N=16; interaction F=1.999, p=.163; underwater-learned items were recalled better on land). Original interaction F=22.0 implies d>=2.7, implausibly large for a small sample. Original had 16 amateur-diver undergraduates over 4 days; the replication was done in about 1.5 h and its preregistration was filed after data analysis (in-principle acceptance only), so it is not a clean preregistered replication.
agent_test: None needed; treat the naturalistic proof as unreliable.

claim: Context effects shrink when other cues are available or items are associated at study (associative processing d=.13 vs nonassociative .33; outshining/overshadowing), and vanish with decontextualised real-world use (Saufley: 21 classroom comparisons, none reliable).
agent_test: Compare context-tagged vs untagged memory when the query already names the item (expect no gain) and when it does not.
audit_note: Smith and Vela (associative .13 vs nonassociative .33, chi2 6.67) and Saufley et al. (21 comparisons, seven courses, none reliable) verified; 'vanish with real-world use' generalises from one university study, and overshadowing/outshining are Smith and Vela's own hypotheses.

claim: Context reinstatement effects can be very large when each context cues few items, and fall with cue overload (video context d=3.02 at 1 word per scene, 2.18 at 3, 1.00 at 15).
agent_test: Index memory so each key maps to few items; measure recall vs items per key.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Cue diagnostic value (how few traces a cue fits), not raw encoding-retrieval match, drives cued recall: higher match helped only at low overload (.37 vs .24; .28 vs .28 at high overload), and a studied weak cue still beat a strong unstudied one (.32 vs .25).
agent_test: Ablate: add matching but non-unique keys vs unique keys to notes; expect only unique keys to help.
audit_note: Goh and Lu (.37 vs .24, .28 vs .28, .32 vs .25) verified; Poirier et al. (Nairne lab) is independent and consistent but tests response time, not the recall numbers. Interpretive 'drives' is the authors' account; Exp 2 shows match still helped at low overload.

claim: Accuracy falls with the number of items sharing a cue (fan): humans 91.2/82.4/71.8% at fan 1/2/4 versus dense retrieval 94.1/76.3/58.2/44.7% at fan 1/2/4/8; a hippocampus-style graph retriever sits near humans.
agent_test: Run fan-controlled retrieval with dense vs graph/entity index at equal context tokens. c06 is one preprint with its own human sample.

claim: Agent memory that writes a scene/context trace with each fact improves cross-session QA where traces must be separated or ordered: 73.7% vs 53.5% (+20.2 pp, n=99 pairs) on LongMemEval-S, no gain on single-session facts (75 vs 75).
agent_test: Replicate with another model and a scene-at-retrieval ablation at equal tokens. One preprint, one run.

claim: Widening the cues kept at write time helps retrieval: key=value+extracted fact beats value-only keys (Recall@5 0.644 vs 0.582 at round level), document expansion with predicted queries raised Recall@1000 85.3 to 89.3, and A-MEM note enrichment lifted temporal F1 45.85 vs 25.52 for MemGPT. Counter-evidence: expansion with LLM text hurt strong retrievers across 24 models (Weller), and on LoCoMo raw chunks matched or beat LLM-rewritten facts and summaries (Yuan: 77.9/59.2/81.1 raw vs 72.2/49.4/77.3 facts, cosine/BM25/hybrid). Gains depend on retriever strength and on keeping the raw text.
agent_test: Write-time enrichment ablation: raw note vs note+keywords+likely questions, equal tokens. Keep original wording as a key.

claim: Moving the query toward the stored form helps: HyDE nDCG@10 61.3 vs Contriever 44.5 and BM25 50.6 on TREC DL19; time-aware query expansion raised recall 11.3% (round) but only when a strong model made the time range. Caveat: HyDE gains were concentrated in claims where the generated text already held entailed gold evidence (FEVER Recall@5 40.0 matched vs 23.4 unmatched vs 26.8 Contriever baseline), i.e. it helps only when the guess of the stored form is right.
agent_test: Query rewrite into the stored format before retrieval vs raw query at equal tokens, strong vs weak rewriter.
audit_note: HyDE table, LongMemEval 11.3% (round) with strong-LLM caveat, and Yoon et al. FEVER Recall@5 40.0/23.4/26.8 verified; Weller not opened.

claim: Parametric memory is cue-direction dependent: GPT-3 trained on Name-is-Description gets 0.0% on the reverse question (DescriptionToName 96.7% same vs 0.1% reverse); the same fact in context is reversible; varied-wording pretraining raised QA from 9.7% to 96.6%. In the short-context case the reversal works: 3-shot GPT-3 reached 100% (96.67% at 350M) on in-context reversal, so the lock is parametric; long-context retrieved text is untested.
agent_test: Do not rely on the model to retrieve a fact by a different cue than it was written with; put the needed fact in context in the query direction.
audit_note: Berglund (96.7/0.1, 0.0, in-context 100/96.67 and footnote) and Allen-Zhu (9.7% to 96.6%) verified; the closing 'long-context retrieved text is untested' is an absence claim.

claim: Transformer attention can be read as cue-based retrieval: swapping K+V made every tested model hallucinate on 100% of factual prompts, K alone left accuracy near 30-40%, and perturbing identified keywords hurts verbatim recall more than random tokens (except Llama 2).
agent_test: Interpretive analogy from one preprint on open models and memorised book text; low priority.

claim: A 7B model on Tulving-style designs diverges from humans: delayed recall from the copy word was 0 words though immediate recognition was perfect, and associative cues beat rhyme cues far more than in humans.
agent_test: One author, one small model; rerun on a frontier model before generalising.

claim: Placement matters for provided evidence: accuracy is lowest when the answer is mid-context (GPT-3.5 drops more than 20 pp). Interaction with match: hard distractors do more harm at prompt edges than in the middle (36-44% vs 28-34% distracting effect), and in real retrieval reordering by position preference equals random shuffle (Qwen 7B 71.73 max-relevance vs 71.00 shuffle).
agent_test: Place retrieved lessons at start or end of the prompt vs middle at equal tokens.
audit_note: Liu et al. says 'more than 20%' (the 30-document table shows about 23 pp between first and middle slot, so pp is consistent) and Cuconasu et al. numbers (36-44% vs 28-34%, Qwen 7B 71.73 vs 71.00) verified; Cuconasu itself concludes position bias matters little in real retrieval.

claim: Transfer-appropriate processing and recognition failure of recallable words extend the match idea to processes and to recognition checks.
agent_test: Primary papers (Morris 1977, Tulving and Wiseman 1975, Tulving and Thomson 1973) unread; verify before use.

claim: Varied use across contexts makes memory cue-independent only when each use is a real retrieval attempt: Smith and Handy (2014) final recall 2 days later constant .43 vs varied .61 (Exp 1, N=45, d=.71); with restudy instead of retrieval practice no benefit (Exp 4, N=36, constant .51 vs varied .36, ns). Saufley classroom null still stands. Processing at input also matters (Smith 1986: recognition context effects only after short-term-maintenance input).
agent_test: Retrieve and use a note under many different query phrasings or task contexts (real retrieval attempts) vs the same phrasing; also a re-read-only arm. Measure retrieval with a fresh phrasing.

claim: Context-dependent recall appears in VR with very different worlds (same .32 vs different .26, N=64), larger for world-relevant items, with no clear effect at immediate test.
agent_test: Small effect from one study; does not change design.

claim: Generic agent retrieval scored by recency, importance and relevance helps believability but the three terms were never ablated separately, so the cue-match share is unmeasured.
agent_test: Ablate relevance, recency and importance separately on a distractor task at equal tokens.

claim: Retrieved passages that are semantically close to the question but lack the answer cost an LLM reader more than unrelated ones: Llama2-7b 0.5642 gold-only to 0.4068/0.3815/0.3626 with 1/2/4 ADORE distractors, while random passages placed next to the query raised accuracy by up to 0.08 (+36%); hard distractors cost 6 to 11 accuracy points depending on the LLM, and the cost persists for Llama-3.3-70B; in Llama-2-13B, manual review of 240 failures found retrieval caused the error in 73% (65-85% by setting), and with low-ranked context the wrong answer entity appeared in the retrieved text in 77% of NQ errors (37% with random context).
agent_test: Score each retrieved lesson for distraction (answer vs abstain on it alone) and drop high scorers; compare with random-lesson padding at equal tokens.
audit_note: Cuconasu (0.5642 to 0.4068/0.3815/0.3626, +0.08 / +36% from random docs) and Amiraz (6 to 11 points, persists for Llama-3.3-70B, range is across LLMs not 70B alone) match, but Yoran et al. say retrieval caused the error in 73% of 240 manually annotated failures, and separately that in 77% of NQ errors with low-ranked context the wrong entity appeared in the retrieved text; the claim merges these into '73% of retrieval-caused errors copied an entity ... (77%)'.
claim_before_audit: Retrieved passages that are semantically close to the question but lack the answer cost an LLM reader more than unrelated ones: Llama2-7b 0.5642 gold-only to 0.4068/0.3815/0.3626 with 1/2/4 ADORE distractors, while random passages next to the query raised accuracy up to +36%; hard distractors cost 6-11 points even for a 70B model; 73% of retrieval-caused errors in Llama-2-13B copied an entity from the mismatched passage in the low-rank case (77%).

claim: For frontier models the cost of wrong retrieval can be very large: with Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro, when all retrieved passages were wrong (RGB worst case) plain RAG was more than 50 points below no-RAG, and about 70% of retrieved passages lacked the answer in the realistic setting. A source-aware consolidation prompt was the only method near the no-RAG level.
agent_test: Add a consolidate-with-source-labels step before using retrieved lessons; test with all-wrong retrieval as the worst case.

claim: LLM expansion of queries or documents helps weak retrievers and hurts strong ones (11 methods, 12 datasets, 24 models; negative correlation between baseline and gain; 28 of 28 hand-checked non-label failures were added irrelevant terms). The extra-token control (random vs matched keys) is still missing for agent notes.
agent_test: Run enrichment against plain, random-token and wrong-key arms with the strongest retriever the agent will use.
audit_note: Weller et al. (11 methods, 12 datasets, 24 models, negative correlation, 28 of 28 non-label failures from irrelevant/erroneous added terms) verified; the 28/28 comes from a hand sample of only 30 failures from three datasets, and Yuan et al.'s abstract and the Anthropic post do not bear on the expansion-hurts-strong-retrievers claim. Absence statement about agent notes not checkable.

claim: On LoCoMo (GPT-5-mini, 1,540 questions) retrieval method moves accuracy by 14-23 points while write strategy moves it by 3-8; raw chunks (zero LLM write cost) matched or beat extracted facts and summaries; retrieval precision@5 correlates r=0.98 with accuracy; utilization failures stay at 4-8%.
agent_test: Keep the raw text in every note; add enrichment as extra keys beside it, not instead of it.

claim: Index-time context prefixes (about 100 tokens per chunk) cut top-20 retrieval failures from 5.7% to 3.7% (embeddings), 2.9% (plus BM25) and 1.9% (plus reranking); vendor report, no random-prefix control.
agent_test: Replicate with a same-length random prefix and a wrong-document prefix arm.

claim: HyDE-style query rewriting works through the model already knowing the stored form: with GPT-4o-mini on FEVER, Recall@5 was 40.0 when the generated text held entailed evidence and 23.4 when it did not, below the 26.8 baseline. On private agent notes the model has not seen the text, so this bet may fail.
agent_test: Compare query rewriting against storing 2-3 forms per note on a private-note benchmark at equal tokens.

claim: A fit check before use reduces the harm of mismatched retrieved items but costs some useful ones: NLI entailment filtering prevented the loss in Llama-2-13B but discarded relevant passages; Chain-of-Note judgement notes gave +7.9 EM at 100% noise and +2.7 at 0% noise (LLaMa-2 7B fine-tuned); source-aware consolidation helped Claude and Gemini. No direct test of a cues-are-associates warning or forced-answer-then-score exists.
agent_test: Test a one-line condition-match check per retrieved lesson against no check, measuring both harm avoided and lessons lost.
audit_note: Yoran NLI filtering (prevents loss, discards relevant passages), Chain-of-Note +7.9 EM at fully noisy retrieval (+2.7 at 0% noise not located in the text read) and Astute RAG (Claude/Gemini) verified in abstracts/text; CoN is a note-writing relevance judgement rather than a pure pre-use filter, and the closing absence claim is not checkable.

claim: Ordering retrieved items by model position preference does not help in realistic retrieval, because relevant and highly distracting passages sit near the top together (over 60% of queries had at least one highly distracting passage in the top 10); effort belongs in filtering mismatches.
agent_test: Do not spend scaffold tokens on re-ordering lessons; spend them on a mismatch filter.
